name: Royal Academy of Arts
description: Britain's first art school, founded 1768, hosting the Summer Exhibition and blockbuster shows in Burlington House on Piccadilly.
tips: The Summer Exhibition (June-August) is the longest-running open-submission show in the world.

name: Faraday Museum at the Royal Institution
description: Basement laboratory where Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetism, preserved exactly as he left it, plus science history galleries.
tips: Free entry. Tuesdays at 1pm there are often free science demonstrations in the historic lecture theatre.

name: Handel & Hendrix in London
description: Two musicians separated by 200 years lived in adjoining Mayfair houses — Handel upstairs, Hendrix next door. Both are now a museum.
tips: Jimi Hendrix's flat has been restored to 1969, complete with his guitars and album collection.

name: Benjamin Franklin House
description: The only surviving home of Benjamin Franklin — he lived here 1757-1775. Now a museum offering an immersive 'Historical Experience' tour.
tips: Book ahead — tours are small-group and often sell out.

name: Dr Johnson's House
description: Home of Samuel Johnson while he compiled his landmark 1755 Dictionary of the English Language. A Queen Anne townhouse hidden off Fleet Street.
tips: Hidden down an alley off Fleet Street. Don't miss the statue of Johnson's cat Hodge outside.

name: 18 Stafford Terrace (Sambourne House)
description: Victorian artist Linley Sambourne's home, preserved virtually untouched since 1874 — a perfect time capsule of Aesthetic Movement taste.
tips: Open Wednesday-Sunday only. Book ahead — timed entry.

name: Freud Museum London
description: Sigmund Freud's final home, where he fled from Nazi-occupied Vienna in 1938. His study and famous couch are preserved exactly as he left them.
tips: The couch is smaller than you'd think. Closed Monday-Tuesday.

name: Fenton House
description: 17th-century merchant's house on Hampstead's highest point, with orchard, walled garden, and a world-class collection of early keyboard instruments.
tips: National Trust — free for members. Concerts on the historic harpsichords happen monthly.

name: Jewish Museum London
description: The story of Jewish life in Britain from 1066 to today, including medieval artefacts and a reconstructed East End tailor's workshop.
address: Raymond Burton House, 129-131 Albert St, London NW1 7NB
tips: Collection relocated — check current venue before visiting.

name: Museum of Brands, Packaging & Advertising
description: Over 12,000 items of British consumer culture arranged chronologically — from Victorian soap to 1990s cereal boxes. A powerful nostalgia trip.
tips: Pair with Portobello Road Market — 5 minutes away.

name: Florence Nightingale Museum
description: The story of the founder of modern nursing, inside St Thomas' Hospital where she established her nursing school in 1860.
address: St Thomas' Hospital, 2 Lambeth Palace Rd, London SE1 7EW
tips: Directly opposite the Houses of Parliament across the river. Combine with a walk along Lambeth.

name: Estorick Collection of Modern Italian Art
description: The only British gallery dedicated to modern Italian art, with outstanding Futurist works by Boccioni, Balla, and Severini in a Georgian house.
tips: Small but perfectly formed. The garden café is a hidden gem.

name: William Morris Gallery
description: The only public museum devoted to the great designer and socialist, in his boyhood Georgian home in Walthamstow.
address: Lloyd Park, Forest Rd, Walthamstow E17 4PP
tips: Free entry. Walthamstow Central is on the Victoria Line — 20 minutes from central.

name: Vagina Museum
description: The world's first bricks-and-mortar museum dedicated to gynaecological anatomy, addressing myths, history, and health with humour and rigour.
tips: Free entry, suggested donation. Check current location before visiting — they've moved several times.

name: The Cinema Museum
description: A vast collection of cinema memorabilia housed in the old Lambeth workhouse where Charlie Chaplin briefly lived as a child.
tips: Access by guided tour only — check website for tour dates.

name: London Silver Vaults
description: Underground vaults built in 1885 and now home to 30+ specialist silver dealers — the world's largest retail collection of antique silver.
tips: Closed Sundays. Free to wander even if you're not buying. The entrance looks like nothing — persist to the vaults below.

name: Clockmakers' Museum
description: The world's oldest collection of clocks and watches — 600 timepieces spanning 500 years — inside the Science Museum's gallery at the Guildhall.
tips: Free. Combine with the adjoining Guildhall Art Gallery and Roman amphitheatre remains.

name: Guildhall Art Gallery
description: The City of London's art collection, including 'The Defeat of the Floating Batteries at Gibraltar', plus Roman amphitheatre remains in the basement.
tips: Don't miss the Roman amphitheatre remains below the gallery — the outline is traced in the courtyard stones above.

name: Ragged School Museum
description: The largest 'ragged school' Dr Barnardo opened for the children of London's poor, preserved as a Victorian classroom and kitchen.
tips: Free. Monthly 'Victorian lesson' days are popular with families — book ahead.

name: The Magic Circle Museum
description: The world's most prestigious society of magicians opens its HQ for public tours — props from Tommy Cooper, Houdini, and Paul Daniels.
tips: Tours only — check website. Some include live magic performances.

name: Twinings Shop & Museum
description: The world's oldest tea shop, operating from the same Strand premises since 1706. Tiny museum at the back tells the family's 300-year history.
tips: Free. The doorway is original Queen Anne — mind your head on the way in.

name: Polish Institute and Sikorski Museum
description: London's Polish government-in-exile during WWII is remembered here, with the finest Polish military history collection outside Poland.
tips: Open Tuesday-Friday and first Saturday of the month. Suggested donation.

name: Hogarth's House
description: The country retreat of 18th-century satirist William Hogarth, preserved with a Georgian garden and original prints including 'A Rake's Progress'.
tips: Free. A tiny oasis beside the A4 Great West Road. Combine with Chiswick House next door.

name: Strawberry Hill House
description: Horace Walpole's 'little Gothic castle' (1749) — the birthplace of Gothic Revival architecture, whimsically turreted and fan-vaulted.
tips: Closed Mondays and Tuesdays. Take the train to Strawberry Hill station.

name: Ham House
description: A near-unaltered 17th-century mansion on the Thames, famously haunted, with sumptuous interiors and one of Europe's finest surviving baroque gardens.
tips: National Trust. Take the Hammerton's Ferry from Marble Hill House across the Thames — one of London's loveliest short boat trips.

name: Marble Hill House
description: A Palladian villa built in 1724 for George II's mistress Henrietta Howard, set in 66 acres of Thames-side parkland.
tips: Park is free and open dawn-dusk. The house interior opens weekends April-October.

name: Rainham Hall
description: A 1729 Georgian merchant's house with a walled garden and tearoom, in a corner of east London most tourists never reach.
tips: National Trust. Accessible from Rainham station (c2c line).

name: Sutton House
description: The oldest surviving house in Hackney — a Tudor red-brick mansion (1535) with carved panelling, a chapel, and a 1980s squatter's graffiti gallery.
tips: National Trust. The café in the Tudor kitchen is lovely.

name: Valentines Mansion
description: A Queen Anne house (1696) in east London with restored period rooms and an 18th-century walled garden, entirely free to visit.
tips: Free. The gardens are a lovely place for a picnic.

name: Red House
description: William Morris's 1860 home — the founding building of the Arts and Crafts movement, designed by Philip Webb with murals by Edward Burne-Jones.
tips: National Trust. Book a guided tour to see the Burne-Jones murals in the drawing room.

name: 2 Willow Road
description: Modernist architect Ernő Goldfinger's 1939 home — a striking three-house terrace he designed, lived in, and kept exactly as he left it.
tips: National Trust. Small tours only — must book. The house name 'Goldfinger' inspired Ian Fleming's villain.

name: Emery Walker's House
description: 7 Hammersmith Terrace — the last surviving Arts and Crafts house interior in Britain, lived in by Morris's collaborator Emery Walker.
tips: Tours only — small groups. Stunning Thames views from the garden.

name: Leyton Hall
description: A Tudor manor surviving in Waltham Forest, surrounded by parkland and hosting changing exhibitions on local history.
tips: Free. Check opening hours before visiting — volunteer-run.

name: All Hallows by the Tower
description: London's oldest church, founded 675 AD. Samuel Pepys watched the Great Fire from its tower; John Quincy Adams married here in 1797.
tips: Free. The crypt museum has a 2,000-year-old Roman pavement.

name: St Mary-le-Bow
description: The Wren church whose famous 'Bow Bells' define a true Cockney. Crypt dates to 1080; current building rebuilt after the Great Fire.
tips: Free. The Café Below in the Norman crypt is a perfect City lunch spot.

name: St Stephen Walbrook
description: Wren's own favourite of his churches — a perfect domed interior that served as the prototype for St Paul's Cathedral.
tips: Free. Henry Moore's controversial stone altar divides visitors — judge for yourself.

name: St Bride's Fleet Street
description: The 'journalists' church' — Wren's tiered-spire church (which inspired the wedding cake) with a crypt museum tracing 2,000 years of Fleet Street.
tips: Free. The choir is renowned — check for free lunchtime concerts.

name: St James's Piccadilly
description: Wren's only from-scratch parish church, with a Grinling Gibbons reredos, weekly organ recitals, and a courtyard antique market.
tips: Free. The courtyard hosts an antiques market Tuesdays, an arts and crafts market Wed-Sat.

name: St Pancras Old Church
description: One of the oldest sites of Christian worship in Britain (possibly 4th century). Graveyard contains the Hardy Tree — an ash with roots among tombstones.
tips: Free. The Hardy Tree (Thomas Hardy arranged gravestones around it as an apprentice architect) fell in 2022 but the site remains poignant.

name: The London Oratory (Brompton Oratory)
description: London's grandest Italianate Catholic church (1884), renowned for its Latin mass and spectacular marble interior.
tips: Free. Sunday 11am Solemn Latin Mass with full choir is extraordinary.

name: Chelsea Old Church
description: Thomas More's private chapel survives from 1528 — one of very few pre-Reformation fragments in London. Bombed in the Blitz, carefully rebuilt.
tips: Free. The Lawrence Chapel contains the sole intact monument to Thomas More's wife.

name: Bevis Marks Synagogue
description: Britain's oldest synagogue still in continuous use (1701), richly oak-panelled, lit by seven magnificent brass candelabras.
tips: Closed Saturdays. Guided tours Monday, Wednesday, Thursday — donations welcome.

name: Methodist Central Hall Westminster
description: The United Nations met here in 1946; Churchill praised it; the organ is one of the largest in Britain. A stunning Edwardian Baroque interior.
tips: Free to enter. Opposite Westminster Abbey — vastly less crowded.

name: London Central Mosque
description: The gleaming copper-domed mosque on the edge of Regent's Park. Non-Muslims welcome — tours by arrangement.
tips: Free. Modest dress expected; headscarves available at the entrance.

name: BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir
description: Britain's first traditional Hindu stone temple — Italian Carrara marble carved in India and assembled in Neasden. Magical.
tips: Free. Modest dress, shoes off. Don't miss the 'Understanding Hinduism' exhibition.

name: Horizon 22
description: London's highest free viewing gallery, on the 58th floor of 22 Bishopsgate. Stunning 360° views of the City, Thames, and beyond.
tips: Free but book ahead — tickets release 2 weeks in advance and go fast.

name: The Garden at 120
description: A rooftop garden on the 15th floor of 120 Fenchurch Street, free to visit, with panoramic City views and wisteria walks.
tips: Free, no booking needed. Open weekdays 10am-6:30pm.

name: Tate Modern Viewing Level
description: Level 10 of the Blavatnik Building offers 360° views of the City skyline, free for anyone visiting Tate Modern.
tips: Free. Sunset over St Paul's from this terrace is one of London's great photo ops.

name: St Paul's Cathedral Golden Gallery
description: Climb 528 steps up the dome to the Golden Gallery at the base of the lantern — the highest public viewpoint in any British cathedral.
tips: Not for the claustrophobic or faint of heart. Pause at the Whispering Gallery halfway up.

name: The Ned — Rooftop Pool & Terrace
description: The old Midland Bank building's rooftop terrace above the City — heated pool, panoramic bar, and panoramic views for members and hotel guests.
tips: Non-members can book Cecconi's or the Lutyens Grill restaurant to access part of the building.

name: Millennium Bridge
description: The elegant steel-cable footbridge linking St Paul's to Tate Modern — London's first new Thames crossing in over a century when it opened in 2000.
tips: Free. Famously 'wobbled' on opening and was immediately nicknamed. Best photos looking north at St Paul's.

name: Albert Bridge
description: Chelsea's candy-pink suspension bridge (1873), strung with 4,000 bulbs at night. Once the most delicate bridge in London — still has 'troops must break step' signs.
tips: Free. Walk across at dusk for the full illuminated effect.

name: Hammersmith Bridge
description: Gilded suspension bridge (1887), currently closed to traffic but open for pedestrians — a Victorian confection admired by the Thames Path.
tips: Free. Best viewed from The Dove pub on the Hammersmith side.

name: Rolling Bridge, Paddington Basin
description: Thomas Heatherwick's extraordinary curling footbridge that rolls into a figure-of-eight every Wednesday at noon and Friday at 2pm.
tips: Free. Show times vary — check the Merchant Square website to avoid missing it.

name: 30 St Mary Axe (The Gherkin)
description: Norman Foster's iconic 41-storey curved-glass tower (2003). Part of the City's skyline quartet with the Cheesegrater, Walkie-Talkie, and Scalpel.
tips: Free to view from outside. Occasionally opens for Open House London — book months ahead.

name: Lloyd's Building
description: Richard Rogers' radical 'inside-out' masterpiece (1986) with lifts and pipes on the outside — the boldest statement of British High-Tech architecture.
tips: Free to view. Interior rarely open — try Open House London weekend in September.

name: The Leadenhall Building (Cheesegrater)
description: Rogers Stirk Harbour's wedge-shaped tower (2014), designed to preserve St Paul's protected sightlines — an engineering masterwork up close.
tips: Free to view. The public atrium on ground floor is often accessible — worth stepping inside to see the yellow X-braces.

name: Battersea Arts Centre
description: A beautifully reimagined Victorian town hall turned theatre and performance space — damaged by fire in 2015, restored with exposed charred timber.
tips: Check 'Scratch' nights — short works-in-progress for £5-10.

name: Bridge Theatre
description: Nicholas Hytner's 900-seat theatre on the Thames near Tower Bridge — London's most ambitious new-build theatre in 80 years.
tips: Standing tickets in some productions from £10. Great views of Tower Bridge from the bar before the show.

name: The Old Vic
description: Britain's oldest continuously operating theatre (1818), home stage to Olivier, Gielgud, and Kevin Spacey. Now under Matthew Warchus.
tips: £10 PwC tickets for under-25s and Lottery tickets 24h before showtime.

name: Young Vic
description: Edgy, experimental theatre in Waterloo, founded by Frank Dunlop in 1970 as a home for young audiences. Consistently innovative programming.
tips: £10 Lucky Dip tickets go on sale 2 weeks ahead.

name: Almeida Theatre
description: Intimate 325-seat theatre in Islington, famous for discovering and reinventing classics. Rupert Goold's productions transfer regularly to West End.
tips: Book early — transfers sell out fast. Under-30s discounts available.

name: Donmar Warehouse
description: A 250-seat studio theatre in Covent Garden — the most intimate high-profile theatre in London, founded by Sam Mendes.
tips: Tiny — every seat is excellent. Barclays £10 tickets via ballot 30 days in advance.

name: Sadler's Wells Theatre
description: The world's leading dance house — contemporary, ballet, flamenco, hip-hop — on a site where a spring-fed theatre first opened in 1683.
tips: Sign up to the mailing list for early-release prices.

name: Regent's Park Open Air Theatre
description: London's only dedicated outdoor theatre, performing each summer since 1932 in a gorgeous woodland setting inside Regent's Park.
tips: Season May-September. Bring a cushion and a waterproof — shows run rain or shine.

name: Wilton's Music Hall
description: The world's oldest surviving grand music hall (1858), saved from demolition and now a haunting, beautiful venue for theatre and gigs.
tips: The Mahogany Bar is worth a drink even without seeing a show.

name: Hackney Empire
description: Frank Matcham's 1901 variety theatre, saved and restored, now London's best panto and one of its most beautiful interiors.
tips: Pantomime season (Nov-Jan) books out months ahead.

name: Royal Court Theatre
description: The writers' theatre of Britain — every major contemporary playwright's work has passed through this Sloane Square stage since 1956.
tips: Monday tickets all £12. The Theatre Upstairs studio (75 seats) is even better.

name: Arcola Theatre
description: A former textile factory in Dalston turned radical, low-carbon fringe theatre with two studios and a café-bar.
tips: Pay-what-you-can Tuesdays. One of the best under-the-radar programmes in London.

name: The Bush Theatre
description: Shepherd's Bush studio theatre in a stunning former library, championing new writers — Jez Butterworth, Jack Thorne, and Lolita Chakrabarti all broke here.
tips: £15 Monday nights. The café is a great pre-show option.

name: Theatre Royal Stratford East
description: Joan Littlewood's legendary East End playhouse — the birthplace of 'Oh, What a Lovely War!' Ornate Victorian auditorium.
tips: Two minutes from Stratford station. Great community programming.

name: Kiln Theatre
description: Kilburn's razor-sharp new-writing theatre (formerly Tricycle), known for plays on race, religion, and politics. Recently redesigned.
tips: Under-26 tickets £10. Paired cinema shows arthouse films.

name: Lyric Hammersmith Theatre
description: A gorgeous Victorian auditorium (1895) hidden inside a 1970s shopping centre — perfectly preserved plasterwork, adventurous programming.
tips: £10 tickets for under-25s. The exterior is modernist; the shock of the Victorian interior is part of the magic.

name: Menier Chocolate Factory
description: Former cocoa warehouse turned off-West-End theatre and restaurant — small but produces musicals that transfer to Broadway.
tips: The dinner+show package is excellent value.

name: Electric Cinema (Notting Hill)
description: Sumptuously restored 1910 picture palace — velvet armchairs, leather sofas, and front-row beds, plus cocktail service to your seat.
tips: The beds at the back (two people, blankets provided) are a treat but book weeks ahead.

name: Rio Cinema Dalston
description: Art Deco gem (1937) still running as an independent picture house, with a famous kids' club and late-night cult classics.
tips: Old Girls' Cinema club on some Thursdays. Saturday kids' club is legendary.

name: The Prince Charles Cinema
description: Leicester Square's cult cinema — all-nighters, sing-alongs, pyjama screenings, and quote-alongs. A London institution.
tips: Membership card pays for itself after 3 visits. Wes Anderson marathons are legendary.

name: BFI Southbank
description: The British Film Institute's mothership — four screens, Mediatheque (free archive viewing), and the London Film Festival's main home.
tips: The Mediatheque is free — browse decades of archive TV and film on individual screens.

name: Ritzy Picturehouse
description: One of Britain's oldest operating cinemas (1911), now five screens above a lively bar — the social heart of Brixton.
address: Brixton Oval, Coldharbour Lane, London SW2 1JG
tips: Balcony seats upstairs are old-school charming.

name: Regent Street Cinema
description: The birthplace of British cinema — the Lumière brothers showed their first public film here in 1896. Restored in 2015 to its Edwardian glory.
tips: The only cinema in London still projecting 35mm regularly.

name: Genesis Cinema
description: A gorgeously restored Victorian cinema in Mile End with five screens, a vintage bar, and all-dayer events.
tips: £6 Bargain Wednesdays. The Art Deco-style bar is open to non-cinemagoers.

name: Phoenix Cinema
description: One of England's oldest continuously operating cinemas (1910) — an Arts and Crafts interior preserved almost intact.
tips: Membership discounts are excellent. Doubles as a community meeting space.

name: The Castle Cinema
description: A 1910s cinema reopened after 60 years of closure — now a tiny two-screen indie picturehouse with a craft-beer bar.
tips: Members of the Castle Club get priority booking. Double features on Saturdays.

name: Speakers' Corner
description: The north-east corner of Hyde Park where anyone has been able to stand up and speak their mind since 1872. Sunday mornings are liveliest.
address: North-east corner of Hyde Park, London W2 2EU
tips: Free. Sundays from 11am have the most speakers (and hecklers). Enter via Marble Arch.

name: Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square
description: Since 1999 the empty plinth in the NW corner of Trafalgar Square has hosted rotating works of contemporary art — from Anthony Gormley to Yinka Shonibare.
tips: Free. The commission changes every 12-18 months.

name: Horse Guards Parade
description: The ceremonial Changing of the Queen's Life Guard happens here at 11am weekdays — less crowded than Buckingham Palace, closer up.
tips: Free. 11am weekdays, 10am Sundays. Dismount inspection at 4pm daily is quieter still.

name: Inns of Court Walk (Temple & Lincoln's Inn)
description: A walk through the medieval legal quarter — Inner Temple, Middle Temple, Lincoln's Inn — with Tudor halls, Dickensian gardens, and Templar history.
tips: Free. Best on weekdays when the barristers are about and gates are open.

name: Somerset House Ice Rink
description: London's most glamorous outdoor ice rink, lit against the 18th-century courtyard each winter (Nov-Jan).
tips: Club Nights with DJs are popular — book a month ahead.

name: Natural History Museum Ice Rink
description: A seasonal rink around the Museum's Romanesque facade, with the Skate-and-Fizz package for the full festive experience.
tips: Open mid-October to mid-January. Stunning after dark.

name: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
description: 560 acres of east London regenerated for 2012, with the ArcelorMittal Orbit slide, velodrome, aquatics centre, and wildflower meadows.
tips: Free park. The Orbit slide (£17.50) is the world's longest tunnel slide.

name: Thames Path National Trail
description: 184 miles of national trail following the Thames — but the central London section (Hampton Court to Woolwich) is the world-class walk.
tips: Free. Richmond-to-Hammersmith is the prettiest rural-feeling section; Tower Bridge-to-Woolwich is the big-infrastructure thrill.

name: Parkland Walk
description: A 4.5-mile linear park along a disused railway line from Finsbury Park to Highgate and Alexandra Palace — London's longest wildlife corridor.
tips: Free. Spot the 'spriggan' sculpture by Marilyn Collins near Holmesdale Rd.

name: Capital Ring Walk
description: A 78-mile waymarked loop through outer London's green spaces — divided into 15 sections, each walkable in a morning.
address: Various — start/end points accessible by tube
tips: Free. Section 10 (South Kenton to Hendon) includes the Welsh Harp reservoir — surprising rural feel.

name: Little Venice to Camden Canal Walk
description: A peaceful 3-mile towpath walk from Little Venice through Regent's Park and London Zoo to Camden Lock — past houseboats, herons, and a pelican.
tips: Free. Or take the water-bus for £10 one way if legs are tired.

name: Limehouse Basin
description: A triangular Georgian dock (1820) where the Regent's Canal meets the Thames — now a marina surrounded by converted warehouse flats.
tips: Free. The Grapes pub (owned by Ian McKellen) is nearby — Dickensian riverside charm.

name: Thames Barrier Park
description: A 22-acre park on the north bank of the Thames with views of the Barrier's gleaming silver hoods — London's first major new park of the 21st century.
tips: Free. Pontoon Dock DLR is closest. The Green Dock sunken garden is striking.

name: Emirates Stadium Tour
description: Behind-the-scenes tour of Arsenal's 60,000-seat home — dressing rooms, press box, pitchside, and the Arsenal Museum.
tips: Self-guided audio tour included. Legends Tours with former players run monthly.

name: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium Tour
description: The most technologically advanced football stadium in Europe — tour the retractable NFL pitch, dressing rooms, and walk the tunnel.
tips: The 'Dare Skywalk' (£25 extra) takes you across the stadium roof — the world's highest stadium walk.
